strengths: The main strength of this paper stands in the nice research idea. There have been different works in theoretical machine learning dealing with learned representations in two-layer networks trained with one step of gradient; this manuscript extends findings in the literature introducing novel data distribution and learning setting.

The paper deals with an interesting topic, namely the deformation of the input data structure induced by a neural network and how it correlates with the training dataset as a single-step GD training is performed.
The setup is quite generic, as the authors considered a two-layer neural network admitting a possible non-convex loss.
As a result, it is found that the 'strength' of the deformation depends on how much the evaluation dataset is similar to the training set.

The paper proposes a quantitative approach to the problem by studying two quantities of interest, namely the alignment and the local elasticity, and show how such quantities indeed depend on the correlation between training database and signal in the input.
The paper provides a rigorous theoretical foundation for alignment and local elasticity in a two-layer neural network with the explicit formula on both metrics.
The analysis is solid and it provides a new perspective on feature learning in neural networks.
Both alignment and local elasticity are interesting concepts in deep learning and this work studies how they emerge during training.
The math is solid and the theoretical results are sufficiently clean that they can be understood rather easily
Understanding scaling limits of feature learning is clearly an important theoretical direction so the topic is timely and worthwhile.
The model setting (conjugate kernel) is an interesting one for questions of feature learning and remains under explored, in my opinion.
The paper also converts the regression setting of Ba et al to a classification task, which could highlight important differences between the two the problems.
Feature learning is an important topic in the theoretical foundations of deep learning.
The alignment phenomenon observed in this paper seems to be interesting and could be useful to explain the success of neural networks.
The setup considered in this paper is a nice one to study feature learning of neural networks.
weaknesses: The presentation of the manuscript is disordered; the authors try to give intuition behind their results, which leads to a confusing exposition that needs to be enhanced.
The paper heavily relies on techniques already proven in other works, raising concerns about the clear elements of novelty.
The numerical illustrations are far from being clear.
Figure 1 is far from being clear, with unclear origin, legend labels (a,b,c,d), undefined symbols $(a_1,a_2)$, undefined sphere and its transformed mapping, and ambiguous grey arrows.
In page 2 the math is not sound; definitions lack consistency, e.g., $c_3, c_4$ not clearly specified in Defs (1.1,1.2) and indices not specified in the sum of Theorems (1.3,1.4).
The concepts of Local Elasticity and Alignment structure are defined only by citing related papers, with no explanation of what these phenomena really are; explanations are unsatisfactory.
The explanation for the CK framework is never provided; authors refer only to related works.
A large part of the technical results should be moved to the appendix to provide more space for intuition; lemmas between Page 6 and 8 could be moved to the appendix.
The related works section should be expanded and possibly compacted with the introduction to provide a broader view.
It is unclear how crucial the learning rate assumption scaling is; reference to [1] extended (Moniri et al. 2024) ...
The numerical illustrations need to be changed; Figures (3,4,5) are not understandable due to small font size.
It would be interesting to observe distribution shift that are not limited to $e\mu$; authors should comment.
Unclear training procedure in Page 5; what does subscript $c$ for the second layer $a_c$ mean?
Minor points: abstract "recall@1"; page 1 phrasing; page 4 recall what is $\beta$.

The quality of the text is very poor, both at the LaTeX editing level and in writing; quantities are often not specified, sentences are broken, notation is not introduced properly, and conventions change between sections, compromising readability.
The discussion of the main theoretical results is minimal and at some point confusing; see the *Questions* section.
What does "11unseen" mean at line 050?
At line 086 $F$ is introduced, but neither the dimension of $x$ nor the dimension of $W$ nor how $\sigma$ acts are clarified.
At line 107 $\beta$ appears and is rescaled by $n\sqrt N$, both unspecified quantities.
Reference to Appendix C for notation clarification is insufficient; too much is deferred to the appendix.
The concept of Evaluation sample is referred to in Definition 1.1 without introduction; similarly $c_3$ and $c_4$ lack context.
Definition of local elasticity is confusing; do conditions depend on ordered pair $(c_3,c_4)$?
Informal statements of Theorems 1.3 and 1.4 hide too many details; some details must be dug out from the Appendix.
Unclear whether orthogonal decomposition required for $\sigma(x)$ at line 167 is the one stated in terms of Hermite polynomials.
Unclear relevance of the sub‑gaussian assumption; Fig 2's relation with product similarity to $\beta$ is not clear and adds confusion.
Inconsistent dimensions for label vector $y$ and $\beta$ at line 202; unclear whether $\beta$ is in $\mathbb R^d$ or $\mathbb R^{d\times2}$.
Reference to the training algorithm is not clear at line 204 as the loss is not specified.
Inconsistent product $XW^\top$ in Eq 2; notation inconsistencies throughout equations.
Possible typo: in the decomposition of the gradient in Eq 4, $a$ should be $a_2$.
Proof of Proposition 4.1 could be improved; proof of Lemma 4.3 is not a genuine proof.
Unclear what $\Theta_{\mathbb P}$ means.
Lemma 5.1 may be a special case of Theorem 5.2.
Theorems 5.3 and 5.4 are core contributions but comment is minimal; expression of alignment depends on quantities defined in the appendix; Eq 11 is unintelligible without the appendix.
Result seems to depend on the specific training dataset through $\beta$; authors should discuss concentration results; unclear if concentration occurs.
Use of the letter [מ] in Theorem 5.3 and ב in Appendix H harms readability; suggest using Latin or Greek letters.
Unclear meaning of "Considering randomness, we assume that the sole term $\mathscr C_{j,k}$ represents the Alignment".
Notation introduced in line 377 is never used in the main text; $F_0(x)$ is equated to both $F_0$ and $F'_0$.
Dataset construction in the *Data generation* paragraph in Section 6 is not clear; hyperplane orientation unclear.
Appendix is written poorly, looks like sketchy notes, rich in typos and poor in comments; example of truncated Gaussian definition is confusing.
Labels in experiment figures are extremely small and almost unreadable.
Unclear role of the separability condition on the training dataset in the theoretical analysis.
Unclear whether Fig 3 and Fig 4 represent only experimental results or also quantitative comparison with theory.
Recall @ 1 performance discussion is unclear; correlation with Alignment results is not obvious.
Unclear role of $\psi_1$ and $\psi_2$; whether multiple instances are run.
Overall the paper lacks clarity, precision, and contains many typographical errors; a re‑reading is recommended to improve grammar and fix evident typos and bad rendering of formulas and citations.
The presentation of the theoretical works needs to be improved; many results are not well discussed in terms of their implications.

The connection between the theoretical results and practical implications for feature learning is not clearly established; lacks concrete examples of how derived metrics can guide design of better algorithms or architectures.
Experiments are limited to simulation data only; should verify conclusions on more complex datasets (e.g., computer vision or NLP) to demonstrate generalizability.
It is unclear how to conclude Theorem 1.3 and 1.4 based on the formal version of Theorem 5.3 and 5.4; need more discussion on the relationship between these results.
The theorems are not sufficiently clear; result seems to only deal with one step of gradient descent after initialization, and theorem statements do not make this clear.
The problem setting only deals with classification and this should be made clear in the abstract.
The work claims to discover a relationship between alignment and local elasticity, but the connection is not evident; co‑occurrence after one step of GD is not a strong enough connection.
The problem setting is also very unclear; it appears only the first layer is being trained, but this is ambiguous.
The problem setting is too restricted (two‑layer net, classification task, one step of GD) and the message is not sufficiently strong or interesting.
Figures are not quite visible; fonts should be a lot larger.
Assumptions, theoretical setting, and analysis are presented extremely unclearly; notation appears without introduction, e.g., distributions $c_3$ and $c_4$ appear without explanation.
The lack of clarity extends to the writing and discussion of related works; the alignment and local elasticity section is difficult to parse, and statements do not help to contextualize the results.
The main contribution is not identified; informal theorems essentially state known facts and are not presented as novel.
Formal theorem statements are less precise; variables are deferred to the appendix, making them uninterpretable.
Lack of rigor: assumptions are not stated; e.g., Theorem 5.3 lacks introduced notation, appendix has formatting and typos, undermining credibility.
Motivation to study alignment and local elasticity is missing; the paper fails to show why feature learning is important for better generalization.
The machinery used is mainly developed by Ba et al. (2022); no interesting new techniques are introduced.
Writing needs improvement; difficult to understand.
Definitions 1.1 and 1.2 are not sufficiently formal.
Unclear why Theorem 1.3 and 1.4 hold with probability; source of randomness is not explained.
Unclear how to see the improvement of alignment through the arguments in Theorem 5.3 and 5.4.

Many typos and missing periods (e.g., Line 050 11unseen; Line 168 extra period after $Hn(x)$; Line 202 datum; Line 202 the first y is a column vector but the second y is a row vector; Line 226 missing period; Line 298 no space between let and $\alpha$; Line 309, 311, 315 missing period).
